title: Last Stone Wins, Take Up to Three
statement:
There is one pile of n stones. You and a friend take turns, and you move first. On each turn the player removes 1, 2 or 3 stones from the pile. Whoever takes the last stone wins.

Both players play perfectly. Return true if you can force a win, and false otherwise.

examples.why: Take 3, leaving 4. Whatever your friend takes (1–3), you can take the rest.
Whatever you take leaves 5, 6 or 7, and from each of those your friend can leave you 4, which is a lost position.

hints: Work out the answer by hand for n = 1 to 8. Which positions are losing for the player to move?
A position is winning if some move leads to a losing position. With 4 stones, every move hands your friend 1, 2 or 3 stones.
If the pile is a multiple of 4, your friend can always answer your take of k stones with 4 − k. Otherwise you take n mod 4 and become that friend.

explain.intuition:
Call a pile size losing if the player about to move loses with perfect play. Zero stones is losing (the previous player just took the last one). A size is winning when some move reaches a losing size. Filling this in: 1, 2, 3 win, 4 loses, 5, 6, 7 win (each can reach 4), 8 loses, and so on.

The pattern has a simple reason. On a multiple of 4, whatever you take (k), the opponent takes 4 − k and the pile is a multiple of 4 again, until it hits 0 on their move. So you win exactly when n % 4 != 0: take n % 4 stones and put your opponent in that trap.
steps: Notice that a pile of 0 is lost for the player to move.
A pile is won if one of the moves (take 1, 2 or 3) leaves a lost pile.
Filling the table shows that every multiple of 4 is lost and every other size is won.
pitfalls: Writing a recursion or table up to n. With n up to about 2 billion that is far too slow and too much memory.
Getting the base case backwards: with 0 stones the player to move has already lost.

solutions.title: Win/lose table
solutions.idea: Fill win[i] from the bottom: i is won if i − 1, i − 2 or i − 3 is lost. Only the last three values are needed.

solutions.title: Multiples of four lose
solutions.idea: The opponent can mirror every take of k with 4 − k, so multiples of 4 lose and everything else wins.

followups: Each turn may remove 1 to m stones. What is the rule now?
There are several piles and a move takes any number of stones from one pile. How does XOR decide the winner?
